principles: You work with engineers, not account managers.
principleNotes: No layer between you and the work. Questions go to the person who can answer them.
Changes ship in small pieces you can review, so nothing big lands as a surprise.
Launch is the start of the product's life, so we plan for what comes after it.

stages.title: Discover
stages.body: We map the problem, the users and the constraints, and agree on what done looks like.
stages.happens: Conversations with you and, where possible, the people who'll use the product. We look at what exists today, the data and the systems it has to work with.
get: A written scope and success criteria
The risks, and how we'll reduce them
stages.need: Time with the decision-maker, access to existing systems and data, and a few real users to talk to.

stages.title: Design
stages.body: Flows and screens you can click through before we write production code.
stages.happens: User flows, then a clickable prototype of the main tasks, tested with people who'll use it. The visual design and component system follow.
get: A prototype you can tap through
Screens for every state, phone and desktop
A design system in Figma and code
stages.need: Fast feedback on the prototype, ideally within a day or two of each review.

stages.title: Build
stages.body: Weekly releases to a staging link. You see progress in the product itself.
stages.happens: Small, reviewed changes shipped every week to a staging environment you can open at any time, with a short demo of what moved.
get: Tests on the paths that matter
stages.need: Someone who can say yes or no to scope questions within the week.

stages.title: Operate
stages.body: Launch, monitoring and iteration. We stay on after go-live.
stages.happens: Launch with monitoring and alerts in place, then fixes and the next round of improvements based on how people actually use it.
get: A launch checklist, run with you
Docs and recorded walkthroughs for your team
stages.need: A view on what to improve next, from your users and your numbers.

rhythm.what: Agree the week's goals and anything blocking them.
Short written updates in a shared channel; questions answered the same working day.
A release to staging and a short demo of what changed.

ai-product-engineering.title: AI product engineering
ai-product-engineering.body: LLM features, agents, retrieval and automations designed around real user tasks, with cost, latency and evaluation measured from the first release.
ai-product-engineering.description: LLM features, agents, retrieval and automations built into your product, with evaluation, cost and latency measured from the first release.
headline: AI features your
customers rely on.
ai-product-engineering.imageAlt: Glass and graphite tiles in a grid around a brightly glowing blue core tile
ai-product-engineering.problem: Most AI features stall between a good demo and something customers trust. What closes the gap is rarely the model: it's an evaluation set, cost and latency budgets, permissions, fallbacks and monitoring.

deliverables.title: LLM features in your product
deliverables.body: Assistants, search, drafting, extraction and classification, built into the screens people already use.

deliverables.title: Agents and automations
deliverables.body: Workflows that call your APIs and tools, with approval steps where a mistake would be expensive.

deliverables.title: Retrieval over your data
deliverables.body: Answers grounded in your documents and database, with sources shown and access rules respected.

deliverables.title: Evaluation suites
deliverables.body: Real examples, scored automatically on every change, so quality is measured before a release, not after.

deliverables.title: Cost and latency budgets
deliverables.body: Model routing, caching and limits per task, with spend and response time tracked in production.

deliverables.title: Guardrails
deliverables.body: Content filters, personal-data handling and audit logs, designed in from the start.

approach.title: Start from a task
approach.body: We pick one job a user does today and define what a good result looks like before choosing a model.

approach.title: Build the eval set first
approach.body: Examples from real use become the test suite every prompt and model change has to pass.

approach.title: Ship to a small group
approach.body: The feature goes out behind a flag, with feedback and outputs logged from day one.

approach.title: Measure, then widen
approach.body: Quality, cost per task and latency decide when it reaches everyone.

proof.label: From our founder's work
proof.body: Our founder, Pablo Italo, built a controlled AI assistant for Iluy.ai with model routing, content filters and access across several channels.

questions.a: Usually more than one. We choose per task on measured quality, cost and latency, and keep the choice swappable so a better or cheaper model is a configuration change, not a rewrite.

questions.q: Will our data be used to train models?
questions.a: We build on the providers' business APIs, which don't train on your data by default. When data can't leave your infrastructure, we design for self-hosted models.

questions.q: How do we know it works?
questions.a: An evaluation set built from real examples, scored on every change, plus monitoring and review of live outputs once it ships.

saas-platforms.title: SaaS platforms
saas-platforms.body: Multi-tenant apps, dashboards, billing, APIs and the cloud infrastructure underneath them, built to grow without a rewrite.
saas-platforms.description: Multi-tenant SaaS apps with accounts, teams, billing, APIs and admin tools, on cloud infrastructure built to grow without a rewrite.
headline: SaaS that grows
without a rewrite.
saas-platforms.imageAlt: Three layers of glass and graphite tiles stacked above each other, a blue tile glowing in the middle layer
saas-platforms.problem: A SaaS product is the feature customers see plus a lot they don't: accounts, teams, roles, billing, emails, admin tools, backups. Getting those foundations right early is what lets the product grow without starting over.

deliverables.title: Accounts, teams and roles
deliverables.body: Multi-tenant data model, sign-in with email or Google, invitations and permissions.

deliverables.title: Subscriptions and billing
deliverables.body: Plans, trials, upgrades, failed payments and invoices on Stripe, tested end to end.

deliverables.title: APIs and integrations
deliverables.body: Public APIs, webhooks and connections to the tools your customers use, from calendars to WhatsApp.

deliverables.title: Dashboards and admin
deliverables.body: Reporting for your customers and internal tools for support, so your team doesn't need a developer to help a user.

deliverables.title: Infrastructure
deliverables.body: Containers, CI/CD, staging, backups and monitoring on AWS or the provider you already use.

deliverables.title: Security basics, done
deliverables.body: Least-privilege access, secrets management, audit trails, and data export and deletion for your users.

approach.title: Data model first
approach.body: Tenancy, permissions and billing shape everything else, so we design them before the first screen.

approach.title: One deployable app
approach.body: A well-structured monolith ships faster and is easier to run. Services split out only when load or teams demand it.

approach.title: Staging from week one
approach.body: Every change runs in a production-like environment you can open and try.

approach.title: Observability before launch
approach.body: Errors, logs and key metrics are wired up before real customers arrive.

proof.label: Case study
proof.body: SkedEz, our own booking platform: multi-tenant accounts and teams, Stripe subscriptions, Google Calendar and WhatsApp integrations, in production.

questions.q: How do you avoid a rewrite later?
questions.a: By getting tenancy, permissions and billing right first, keeping the codebase modular, and adding complexity such as queues or separate services only when there's a measured need.
AWS or the provider you already use. Everything runs in containers, so the product isn't tied to one host.
Plans, trials, upgrades and downgrades, failed payments and retries, invoices and taxes, plus the webhooks that keep your database in step with Stripe. We test those paths end to end.

web-and-mobile-apps.title: Web and mobile apps
web-and-mobile-apps.body: Fast websites, web apps, and iOS and Android apps, sharing one codebase where it makes sense and going native where it doesn't.
web-and-mobile-apps.description: Websites, web apps and iOS and Android apps, sharing one codebase where it helps and going native where it matters.
headline: On the web and
in every pocket.
web-and-mobile-apps.imageAlt: A wide frosted glass slab and a tall glass slab, each holding tiles, one blue tile in each
web-and-mobile-apps.problem: You need the product on the web and on phones, without paying to build and maintain it three times, and without an app that feels like a website in a frame.

deliverables.title: Websites and web apps
deliverables.body: Fast, accessible and easy to find in search, built with Next.js and React.

deliverables.title: iOS and Android from one codebase
deliverables.body: React Native with Expo, so most features ship to both platforms at once.

deliverables.title: Native where it matters
deliverables.body: Native modules for camera, sensors, widgets or anything performance-critical.

deliverables.title: Sign-in, payments, notifications
deliverables.body: Google and Apple sign-in, in-app purchases and subscriptions, push notifications.

deliverables.title: Store release
deliverables.body: App Store and Google Play builds, listings and over-the-air updates for fixes between releases.

deliverables.title: Performance and accessibility
deliverables.body: Fast first load, smooth scrolling, screen-reader labels and touch targets that fit a thumb.

approach.title: Share what helps
approach.body: Business logic, design system and most screens are shared; platform conventions are respected.

approach.title: Go native when needed
approach.body: When a shared approach would compromise the experience, that part is written natively.

approach.title: Release pipeline early
approach.body: Builds, test devices and update channels are set up in the first weeks, not the last.

approach.title: Test on real devices
approach.body: Every release is checked on real phones, not only in simulators.

proof.label: Case study
proof.body: SkedEz's app is one cross-platform codebase, built for the web first and ready for the app stores, alongside a Next.js marketing site.

questions.a: Cross-platform for most products, because one codebase is faster to build and cheaper to maintain. Native for apps that live on device features or need the last bit of performance. Often it's a mix.

questions.q: Do you handle the app store release?
questions.a: Yes: builds, signing, store listings and review submissions, set up under your own developer accounts.

questions.q: Can the website and the app share code?
questions.a: Yes. Types, API clients, validation and the design tokens are shared, so a change lands everywhere at once.

product-design.title: Product design
product-design.body: Research, flows, interface design and design systems, done by the people who build them, so nothing gets lost in handoff.
product-design.description: Research, user flows, interface design and design systems, by the people who also build them, so nothing gets lost in handoff.
headline: Designed by the people
who build it.
product-design.imageAlt: Glass, frosted and graphite tiles floating apart at different heights, one glowing blue
product-design.problem: Designs that look right in a file and break in code cost twice. When the people who design the product also build it, the handoff, and most of what gets lost in it, disappears.

deliverables.title: Research
deliverables.body: Interviews and reviews of how people work today, turned into a short list of problems worth solving.

deliverables.title: Flows and wireframes
deliverables.body: The path through each task, agreed before anyone argues about colours.

deliverables.title: Clickable prototypes
deliverables.body: Something you can tap through and put in front of users before code is written.

deliverables.title: Interface design
deliverables.body: Every screen and state, including empty, loading and error, at phone and desktop sizes.

deliverables.title: Design systems
deliverables.body: Tokens, components and guidelines kept in step in Figma and in code.

deliverables.title: Brand for products
deliverables.body: Logos, colour, type and motion that work inside an interface, like this site's.

approach.title: Map the task
approach.body: Who uses it, what they're trying to get done, and where it goes wrong today.

approach.title: Prototype before code
approach.body: Flows are clicked through and tested while changes are still cheap.

approach.title: Finish details in the browser
approach.body: Spacing, motion and responsive behaviour are tuned in the real thing.

approach.title: One system
approach.body: Design tokens drive both Figma and the codebase, so they don't drift apart.

proof.label: Our own work
proof.body: The StationByte brand, this website and its motion system were designed and built in-house, from the logo grid to the glass film in the hero.

questions.q: Can you work from our existing brand?
questions.a: Yes. We extend what you have into a product design system, and only suggest changes where the brand doesn't hold up on screen.

questions.q: Do we get the design files?
questions.a: Yes. Figma files, components and tokens are handed over with the code, in your accounts.

questions.q: Do you test with real users?
questions.a: Yes, with prototypes before build and with the live product after. A handful of sessions catches most of the problems that matter.

skedez.description: How StationByte designed, built and runs SkedEz, online booking for service businesses: booking pages, reminders, Google Calendar, teams and subscriptions.
skedez.summary: Online booking for service businesses. We designed, built and run it, from the database to the reminders.
skedez.problem: Hair salons, physiotherapists, personal trainers and consultants lose hours to back-and-forth messages about times, and to clients who forget. Many booking tools take a commission on each booking or charge per client. We wanted one that does neither, and that a business can set up on its own.

built.title: A booking page per business
built.body: Shared as a link in a bio, a Google profile or a website. Clients pick a service and any free time.

built.title: Reminders that send themselves
built.body: Email 24 hours and 1 hour before every booking on all plans, and WhatsApp on paid plans.

built.title: Google Calendar
built.body: On paid plans, bookings land in Google Calendar, with a Google Meet link when the service is online.

built.title: Teams
built.body: Up to 20 people, each with their own services and working hours.

built.title: Clients
built.body: A client list with CSV import, export any time, and a dashboard of bookings, cancellations and clients.

built.title: Six languages
built.body: Booking pages in English, Portuguese, Spanish, French, German and Italian.

built.title: Plans and billing
built.body: Free, Pro and Teams plans with a 15-day trial on paid plans, no commission on bookings.

built.title: Privacy built in
built.body: Data export and account deletion from the settings, no support ticket needed.

notes.title: Billing tested like it's money, because it is
notes.body: Checkout, plan changes and failed payments are covered by end-to-end tests, so money never depends on a manual check.

notes.title: One codebase for the app
notes.body: One cross-platform codebase serves the web app and is ready for iOS and Android, so a feature is built once.

notes.title: Self-serve from the first minute
notes.body: A business creates its booking page, adds services and shares the link on its own. The free plan needs no card.

pricing.note: 1 person, unlimited services and bookings, WhatsApp, Google Calendar
Up to 20 people, each with their own hours, everything in Pro

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.description: How StationByte LLC collects, uses and protects personal data on stationbyte.com and when you contact us.
privacy.ogAlt: The StationByte tile mark beside the words Your data, kept small
heading: Your data,
kept small.
privacy.lede: We collect only what we need to reply to you and to run this site. No cookies, no analytics, no tracking.

who.title: Who we are
who.p1: This website is run by StationByte LLC (“StationByte”, “we”). We are the controller of the personal data described here. For anything about this policy or your data, write to <mail>contact@stationbyte.com</mail>.

collect.title: What we collect
collect.p1:
When you contact us. If you use the
project form
or email us, we receive your name, email address, what you're building, a budget range if you choose one, your message, and anything else you decide to include.
collect.p2: When you visit. Like most websites, our server records standard technical details for each request: IP address, browser and device type, the page requested and the time. We don't use them to identify you.
collect.p3: Cookies and tracking. This site sets no cookies and uses no analytics, advertising or tracking tools. Fonts, images and video are served from our own server. If you choose a language or close the language suggestion bar, your browser remembers that choice in its own storage; it is never sent to us.

use.title: Why we use it, and on what basis
use.i1: To reply and to prepare a proposal you asked for: steps taken at your request before a possible contract (GDPR Art. 6(1)(b)).
use.i2: To deliver a project if we work together: performance of our contract (Art. 6(1)(b)).
use.i3: To keep the site secure and working, using server logs: our legitimate interest in protecting the site and its visitors (Art. 6(1)(f)).

never.title: What we never do
never.p1: We don't sell your data, share it for advertising, add you to a newsletter, or use it to train AI models.

share.title: Who else handles it
share.p1: Only the providers we need to run the site and answer you: our hosting provider, which stores server logs; our team chat (Slack), which receives project-form submissions; and our email provider, which stores the messages you send us. They process data on our instructions and may not use it for their own purposes.
share.p2: Your data may be processed outside the country where you live. Where the law requires it, we use the safeguards it provides, such as standard contractual clauses.

keep.title: How long we keep it
keep.i1: Enquiries that don't lead to a project: deleted within 12 months of our last message.
keep.i2: Client correspondence: for as long as the work and any legal record-keeping duties require.
keep.i3: Server logs: only as long as needed to keep the site secure, then deleted.

rights.title: Your rights
rights.p1: You can ask us to access, correct, delete or export your data, to restrict how we use it, or object to our use of it. Email <mail>contact@stationbyte.com</mail> and we'll answer within one month. We may need to confirm it's you before acting.
rights.p2: If you're in the EU, the UK or another country with data-protection law, you can also complain to your local data-protection authority. We'd appreciate the chance to fix it first.

security.title: Security
security.p1: The site is served only over HTTPS, and access to messages and servers is limited to the people who need it.

children.title: Children
children.p1: This site is for businesses. It isn't aimed at children, and we don't knowingly collect their data.

changes.title: Changes
changes.p1: If we change how we handle data, we'll update this page and the date at the top.
